title: Homework 2
text:
Task 1:
I am creating the two vectors here. One is for pre_treatment and one is for post_treatment and the vectors contain the blood pressure data.

pre_treatment <- c(130, 128, 116, 124, 133, 134, 118, 126, 114, 127, 141, 138, 128, 140, 137, 131, 120, 128, 139, 135)

post_treatment <- c(114, 98, 113, 99, 107, 116, 113, 111, 119, 117, 101, 119, 130, 122, 106, 106, 124, 102, 117, 113)

# I am storing the created names into an object and applying the automatically generated names to the vector elements.

subject_names <- paste("Subject", 1:20, sep = "_")
names(pre_treatment) <- subject_names
names(post_treatment) <- subject_names

The following code calculates the change in blood pressure for each patient and stores it in a new vector.

bp_change <- pre_treatment - post_treatment

The following code calculates the average decrease in blood pressure across all patients.

mean(bp_change)

Here, I am creating the vectors for the placebo groups.

placebo_pre <- c(138, 135, 147, 117, 152, 134, 114, 121, 131, 130)
placebo_post <- c(105, 136, 123, 130, 134, 143, 135, 139, 120, 124)

  patient = paste("Subject", 1:10, sep = "_"),
  pre_bp = placebo_pre,
  post_bp = placebo_post

Task 4
The following code creates a new column in both data frames called status.

bp_list$treatment$status <- character(20)
bp_list$placebo$status <- character(10)

The following code creates the new status column’s values using a for loop in the placebo data frame.

for (i in 1:20) {
  
  if (bp_list$treatment$post_bp[i] <= 120) {
    bp_list$treatment$status[i] <- "optimal"
    
  } else if (bp_list$treatment$post_bp[i] <= 130) {
    bp_list$treatment$status[i] <- "borderline"
    
  } else {
    bp_list$treatment$status[i] <- "high"
  }
}

The following code does the same thing as the above block but for the non-placebo data frame.

for (i in 1:10) {
  
  if (bp_list$placebo$post_bp[i] <= 120) {
    bp_list$placebo$status[i] <- "optimal"
    
  } else if (bp_list$placebo$post_bp[i] <= 130) {
    bp_list$placebo$status[i] <- "borderline"
    
  } else {
    bp_list$placebo$status[i] <- "high"
  }
}

title: Homework 3
text:
Task 1

I would use this path ../MyData.csv.
The major benefits of using R projects include:


R projects keeps all my different project file types in one folder.
R projects is integrated with tools like Git so I can easily use the terminal to upload and share my work.
R projects provides a nice UI to keep up with all my project files and data in one place.


Git is a version control tool that allows you to track changes in your code on your computer. Github, on the other hand, is a website that allows you to upload these changes to share with others. You can also download (pull) other Github users’ code.
A tibble doesn’t show the entire dataset like a dataframe would when you print it, and it rather shows only rows that fit on the screen. When you access one column of a tibble, it will keep the tibble structure, but when you access one column of a dataframe, it will become a vector.

This is my IQR function which which you can pass unnamed arguments to. IQR is 75th percentile minus 25th percentile.


getIQR <- function(x, ...) {
  q <- quantile(x, probs = c(0.25, 0.75), ...)
  # This line removes the labels on the returned vector result.
  unname(q[2] - q[1])
}

This is my getCoefVar function which you can pass unnamed arguments to. Coefficient of variation is standard deviation divided by the absolute value of mean.


getCoefVar <- function(x, ...) {
  sd(x, ...) / abs(mean(x, ...))
}

Here, I’m creating a function called getSummaries which calls both the IQR and CoefVar functions. There’s no need to rewrite them since we can just call them within this function.


getSummaries <- function(x, ...) {
  # Have to make sure to label them to not get confused.
  c(
    IQR = getIQR(x, ...),
    CoefVar = getCoefVar(x, ...)
  )
}
